analysis.one_liner: Phases out giant factory farms, makes meat companies liable for pollution, and requires country-of-origin labels on meat and dairy.
analysis.headline: The Senate never gave the bill a hearing or a vote; it died in committee when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred new or expanding large concentrated animal feeding operations (giant factory farms) and shut existing ones down by 2040. It would have made the big meat companies that control contract farmers legally responsible for animal waste, pollution, and harm to neighbors. It also would have forced large meatpackers to buy at least half their livestock on the open spot market instead of through their own contracts, and required beef, pork, and dairy to carry honest country-of-origin labels.
analysis.who_benefits: Contract poultry and livestock growers, who borrow heavily to build barns and take on risk under take-it-or-leave-it company contracts, would gain new legal rights and protections. Independent ranchers and farmers would gain because packers could no longer own and feed their own livestock, and would have to buy at least half their animals on the open market. Rural residents living near large factory farms would gain the right to sue the corporations behind them for waste, pollution, and property damage. Consumers would gain clearer labels showing where their meat and dairy come from.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Contract farmers, independent ranchers, rural neighbors

how_it_helps.text: No new large concentrated animal feeding operation could start or expand, and existing ones could not keep operating as large CAFOs after January 1, 2040, with civil penalties up to $10,000 per violation per day.

A program funded with $10 billion every year would pay off debts of animal feeding operation owners who want out and help them convert their land to pasture-based livestock, specialty crops, or organic production.

Meat corporations (integrators) that control contract farms would be legally liable for dead animal disposal, manure, air and water pollution, harm to the contract grower, and health and property losses suffered by neighbors — with attorneys' fees for plaintiffs who win.

Large packers would generally be barred from owning or feeding livestock directly, and would have to buy at least 50% of the animals they slaughter through open spot-market sales from independent producers.

Poultry companies could no longer pay growers through the 'tournament system' when the company itself controls the chicks, feed, and medications that determine a grower's ranking, and could not retaliate against growers who complain or assert their rights.

Mandatory country-of-origin labeling would be restored for beef and pork and extended to dairy, and a 'Product of USA' meat label would be allowed only if the animal was exclusively born, raised, and slaughtered in the United States.

analysis.who_pays: Large meatpackers (a handful of firms slaughter most of the nation's cattle and hogs) and poultry integrators would lose their ability to own livestock, use formula-priced contracts, and shift waste and pollution costs onto contract growers. Operators of large factory farms would face the phase-out. Taxpayers would fund the $10 billion-per-year transition program.

drawbacks.text: The transition program requires $10 billion of automatic funding every year, taken from the Treasury without a separate appropriations vote — a very large, open-ended taxpayer commitment.

Phasing out large CAFOs and forcing half of livestock purchases onto the spot market would raise production costs in an industry built around large-scale, integrated operations, and some of that cost would likely show up in meat prices for consumers; packers also argue formula-priced contracts give them supply security and give producers risk management that open bidding does not. (General knowledge about the industry's economics; not in the provided sources.)

Making integrators strictly liable for pollution and neighbor harm could push companies to reduce the number of contract growing opportunities rather than absorb the new liability, leaving some growers worse off. (General reasoning about how liability rules affect contracting; not in the provided sources.)

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill tackled real, documented problems — water and air pollution from giant feedlots, debt-trapped contract growers, and a meatpacking sector where a few firms dominate. But it was an ambitious, expensive design: a permanent $10 billion per year entitlement, a hard 2040 phase-out of large CAFOs, and a mandate that reshaped how half of all livestock is bought. Honest supporters would concede the price-tag and price-effects were serious and that the bill was written to force a structural fight with the meatpacking industry, not to thread a needle.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Agriculture Committee, which never held a hearing or a vote on it, so it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Cory Booker introduced the bill on July 13, 2021, joined by Senators Warren and Sanders.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry.

That was the only action the bill ever received: it gathered four cosponsors and sat in the Agriculture Committee until the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, with no hearing, no markup, and no vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large meatpackers and poultry integrators are better off: no law now limits packer ownership of livestock, spot-market purchasing, contract terms with growers, or liability for factory farm waste. Contract growers and rural neighbors of large CAFOs remain under the existing rules.

for.name: Sen. Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to place a moratorium on large CAFOs, strengthen the Packers and Stockyards Act, and restore country-of-origin labeling.

for.name: 3 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Sens. Warren and Gillibrand.

for.name: 1 of 2 Senate Independents
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill (Sen. Sanders, named in the introduction).

against.name: Sen. Debbie Stabenow
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing, markup, or vote; it sat in her committee until the Congress ended.

against.name: Large meatpackers and livestock industry groups
against.role: Beef, pork, and poultry processing and trade organizations
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed measures like mandatory country-of-origin labeling and packer ownership restrictions in this era of legislation, reducing appetite for committee action.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat or independent aligned with Democrats (3 of 48 Senate Democrats and 1 of 2 independents), with no Republican support and no committee action under the Democratic chair.

industries.industry: Large meatpackers (cattle, hog, and poultry processing)
industries.note: The bill would bar large packers from owning and feeding livestock and require at least half of their slaughter volume to be bought on the open spot market, directly attacking the vertical integration that locks in their supply. It also limits the formula-priced contracts they use to buy animals cheaply.

industries.industry: Poultry and livestock integrators (companies contracting with growers)
industries.note: Integrators would become strictly liable for waste, pollution, and harm to growers and neighbors — costs the contract-farm model currently pushes onto growers and surrounding communities. Growers would also gain protections against the tournament pay system and retaliation.

New large factory farms could not open or expand, and existing ones would have to stop operating as large CAFOs by 2040, though a federal program would pay off operator debt and fund conversion to other agriculture.

industries.industry: Independent small and mid-size farmers and ranchers
industries.note: Open-market purchase requirements and bans on packer ownership would give independent producers real access to competitive bids, and transition grants would offer an exit from debt-heavy contract farming. These are people rather than a concentrated industry, but they are the bill's intended constituency.

industries.industry: Meat and dairy importers and retailers
industries.note: Mandatory country-of-origin labeling and a 'Product of USA' label restricted to animals born, raised, and slaughtered in the U.S. would add labeling costs and reduce the value of imported meat marketed under U.S. branding.
